To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a new MCP-1/CCl2 competitor, 4F, limits neointima formation in the injured carotid arteries of mice, and that it limits myocardial ischemia reperfusion injury in the mouse.
the novel CCL2/CCR2 inhibitor, CCX354, limits neointima formation after vascular injury and myocardial ischemic injury in mice.

a novel MCP1/CCl2 competitor, 2-[(2S,3R)-3-aminopiperidin-2-yl]-5-(4-chloro-phenyl)-1,2-oxazole, reduces neointima formation after vascular injury in mice, and reduces infarct size after myocardial ischemia and reperfusion in mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new class of chemokine antagonists that may have therapeutic potential in the treatment of inflammatory diseases.
the development of a new class of compounds that can be used to inhibit the chemotactic activity of monocyte chemoattractant proteins, in particular MCP-1/CCL2.
the development of novel therapeutic strategies to limit the extent of neointimal hyperplasia after vascular injury and the severity of myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury (I/R) in the heart.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a new monocyte chemokinetic protein-1/CC motif ligand-3 (MCP-1/CCL3) competitor, CCL3-2, which limits neointima formation after carotid artery ligation in mice, and myocardial infarction and ischemia/reper fusion injury in mice.

our research group has developed a new monocyte chemotractant protein-1/CC chemokine ligand-2 (MCP-1/CCL2) competitor, which is able to limit neointima formation in mice and to reduce myocardial ischemia and reperfusion (MI/R) injury.

we developed and validated a novel, competitive inhibitor of monocyte chemotaxis (MCP-1/CCL2) and demonstrated the therapeutic efficacy of this compound in two models of ischemic heart disease, namely, neointima formation after arterial balloon injury and myocardial ischemic/reperfusion injury.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the monocyte chemotaxis protein-1/CC motif ligand-1 (MCP-1/CCL2) is an important factor in neointima formation.

we have shown for the first time in a mouse model of MI, a new monocyte chemokine CC motif (CCL)2 antagonist, which is able to significantly reduce myocardial ischemic injury, and to limit neointima formation in mice.
we have identified a new chemokine receptor antagonist that has the potential for clinical translation in the treatment of cardiovascular diseases.
